notes.front: What is scalability?
notes.back: How well a system can grow: how easily it can add capacity to do more of what it does.
notes.explanation: There are two ways to scale: add more nodes, or make individual nodes more powerful.
notes.example: A shop website that copes with ten times its usual visitors on sale day because capacity is easy to add.

notes.front: What is horizontal scaling?
notes.back: Increasing a system’s capacity by adding more nodes (more machines running copies of the app), rather than making existing nodes more powerful.
notes.explanation: The work is spread across more machines: if one node handles about 1,000 requests a second, each added node should add about as many.
notes.example: Growing from 4 GB of RAM to 16 GB by adding three more 4 GB nodes.

notes.front: What is vertical scaling?
notes.back: Increasing a system’s capacity by adding CPU and memory to individual nodes; also called “scaling up and down”.
notes.explanation: It lets you resize a server without changing the application’s code.
notes.example: Growing from 4 GB of RAM to 16 GB by switching to a single 16 GB machine.

notes.front: What is autoscaling?
notes.back: A system’s ability to scale automatically, adding resources when needed and removing them when demand falls.
notes.explanation: Systems used to be sized for peak use, which left resources idle; autoscaling lets capacity follow demand instead.
notes.example: A video service adds servers for its Friday-evening viewers and scales back once viewing returns to normal.

notes.front: For a system, what does reliability mean?
notes.back: How well a system responds to failures.
notes.explanation: A distributed system that keeps working as infrastructure changes and components fail is reliable; one that needs people to step in to keep it running is not.
notes.example: A website that carries on serving pages when one of its servers fails.

notes.front: What is portability, as a software characteristic?
notes.back: The ability of software to work in different operating environments without major rework, avoiding “lock-in”.
notes.explanation: Software built for one cloud provider, operating system or vendor is hard to move; portable software adapts with reasonable effort.
notes.example: An app that moves from one cloud provider to another with only small changes.

notes.front: What is observability?
notes.back: How well a system’s outputs let you tell what it is doing, and fix it when something goes wrong.
notes.explanation: Observable systems cut downtime and speed up the response to incidents, so how observable a system is affects its running costs.
notes.example: Seeing on a dashboard that errors jumped straight after a release, and fixing the cause within minutes.

notes.front: What is a system’s desired state?
notes.back: The state you want the system to be in, as distinct from its current (actual) state.
notes.explanation: Much modern automation works by comparing the two and acting to close any gap.
notes.example: Setting a thermostat: the temperature you set is the desired state; the room’s real temperature is the current state.

notes.front: What does it mean to configure a system declaratively?
notes.back: You describe the desired state of the system, without specifying the steps for reaching it.
notes.explanation: This separates the configuration (what you want) from the commands, API calls or scripts used to achieve it.
notes.example: Writing “three copies of this app, version 2” in a file and letting the system work out how.

notes.front: What does it mean to manage a system imperatively?
notes.back: You give it explicit commands, saying what operation to perform, instead of describing the end result.
notes.explanation: Commands make a change in a single step, but they leave no record of previous configurations apart from what is live.
notes.example: Typing “start one more copy of the app” each time you need one.

notes.front: What is a self-healing system?
notes.back: A system that recovers from certain failures without human intervention, by constantly comparing its actual state with the desired state.
notes.explanation: When the two differ, it takes corrective action.
notes.example: Fewer copies of an application are running than the operators asked for, so the system starts new ones.

notes.front: What is a monolithic application?
notes.back: An application with all its functionality in a single deployable program.
notes.explanation: It is often the simplest place to start, but becomes hard to maintain as it grows and more developers change the same code.
notes.example: An online shop whose catalogue, basket and payments are one program, always deployed together.

notes.front: What is the CNCF, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation: part of the Linux Foundation, it looks after Kubernetes and other open source projects for running apps in the cloud.
notes.explanation: Its mission is to make cloud native computing ubiquitous; its Technical Oversight Committee also publishes the definition of cloud native.
notes.example: Kubernetes, the subject of this deck, is a CNCF project.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, “Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)”; CNCF TOC, “Cloud Native Definition”

notes.front: What is a microservices architecture?
notes.back: An approach that breaks an application into independent services, each focused on one function, which together appear to users as one application.
notes.explanation: Each service can be deployed, updated and scaled on its own, and teams can work on their own part without harming the rest.
notes.example: A streaming site with separate services for signing in, searching and playing previews.

notes.front: What does a load balancer do?
notes.back: It spreads incoming requests across several instances of an application, so no single instance gets the bulk of them.
notes.explanation: Horizontally scaled services need something in front of them to share out the traffic; load balancers can be software or hardware.
notes.example: Like a supermarket attendant sending each shopper to the next free till.

notes.front: In the CNCF glossary, what does “service” mean?
notes.back: A microservice: the glossary treats the two words as the same, while noting that “service” has several meanings in IT.
notes.explanation: Whether services and microservices really differ is debated; for a high-level definition, they are treated as one. Kubernetes also has an object called a Service, which is something else (covered later).
notes.example: The search service of a streaming site.

notes.front: What is a tightly coupled architecture?
notes.back: An architecture whose components depend on each other, so that a change in one is likely to affect others.
notes.explanation: It is quicker and simpler to build, but vulnerable to cascading failures and tends to need coordinated rollouts.
notes.example: Changing how a shop’s basket stores prices forces changes to its payment code, and a joint release.

notes.front: What is a loosely coupled architecture?
notes.back: An architecture whose components are built independently, each performing one function that any number of other services can use.
notes.explanation: It is slower to build at first, but teams can develop, deploy and scale their components independently.
notes.example: The search team releases a new version without waiting for the payments team.

notes.front: What is a distributed application?
notes.back: An application whose functionality is broken into several smaller, independent parts, usually microservices, that run in many places.
notes.explanation: It tolerates more failures and can scale horizontally, at the price of more complexity and operational work.
notes.example: A booking site whose search, payments and emails run as separate parts on different machines.

notes.front: What is immutable infrastructure?
notes.back: Infrastructure, such as virtual machines or network appliances, that cannot be changed once deployed; to change it, you replace it.
notes.explanation: Blocking or detecting unauthorised changes makes security risks easier to spot and the system easier to reason about.
notes.example: Instead of patching a running server by hand, you build a new, patched virtual machine and swap it in.

notes.front: What is infrastructure as code?
notes.back: Storing the definition of infrastructure as one or more files, instead of setting it up by hand.
notes.explanation: Infrastructure becomes reproducible, has a single source of truth, and can be kept under version control.
notes.example: A file listing the servers and load balancers a system needs, stored in Git.

notes.front: What is policy as code?
notes.back: Storing policies as files that machines can read and process, instead of documents written only for people.
notes.explanation: Checks become repeatable and less error-prone, and version control records who changed a policy.
notes.example: A policy file forbidding passwords in source code, checked automatically on every change.

notes.front: What is multitenancy?
notes.back: One software installation serving several tenants, each working with its own data.
notes.explanation: Tenants share the installation’s resources without seeing each other’s data, which cuts the cost for everyone.
notes.example: A web email service: millions of users on one installation, none able to read another’s inbox.

notes.front: What is serverless computing?
notes.back: Computing in which servers are hidden from the user: the provider handles machines, provisioning and scaling, and charges per use.
notes.explanation: Unlike IaaS, you do not pay for idle capacity or adjust the number of servers yourself.
notes.example: Uploading code to a provider that runs it only when it is needed and bills you for that use alone.

notes.front: What is Function as a Service (FaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud model that runs individual functions when events trigger them; each runs briefly and then shuts down.
notes.explanation: An instance can start for each request and stop afterwards, so nothing is charged while functions sit idle.
notes.example: Uploading a file triggers a function that converts it into several other formats.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Function as a Service (FaaS)”

notes.front: What is an event-driven architecture?
notes.back: An architecture built around creating, processing and consuming events, an event being any change to an application’s state.
notes.explanation: A central hub routes each event from its producer to the right consumers, which keeps services decoupled.
notes.example: Hailing a ride is an event, routed from your app to the apps of available drivers nearby.

notes.front: What is event streaming?
notes.back: Sending event data continuously from one application to any others that subscribe, describing what it is doing as it happens.
notes.explanation: Opening one connection and letting events flow suits real-time data better than a new request for every event.
notes.example: Stock prices, updated every second, streamed to an app that watches them.

notes.front: What is edge computing?
notes.back: Moving some storage and computing from a central data centre to where the data is produced.
notes.explanation: Processing near the source gives near real-time responses; results are sent back to the data centre afterwards.
notes.example: A self-driving car processing its sensor data on board rather than waiting for a distant data centre.

notes.front: What does “cloud native” mean, in the CNCF’s definition?
notes.back: Practices for developing, building and deploying workloads in public, private or hybrid clouds, at scale, in a programmatic and repeatable way.
notes.explanation: Promoting this approach is the purpose of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), through open source, vendor-neutral projects.
notes.example: A team that deploys its system to any cloud through automated, repeatable definitions instead of servers set up by hand.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: What are cloud native applications?
notes.back: Applications designed to take advantage of cloud computing, using the cloud’s resources and its ability to scale.
notes.explanation: They can run in a cloud provider’s data centre or on cloud native platforms on the organisation’s own premises.
notes.example: An app that restarts automatically after a failure, where an older app needed someone to start it by hand.

notes.front: What are cloud native technologies?
notes.back: The technologies used to build cloud native applications, also called the cloud native stack.
notes.explanation: Together they make it easier to build loosely coupled systems that are resilient, manageable and observable.
notes.example: Microservices and immutable infrastructure are two of them.

notes.front: What is DevOps?
notes.back: A methodology in which one team owns the whole process, from developing an application to running it in production.
notes.explanation: It is a change of culture and process, not just of tools: fewer handoffs between groups mean fewer errors and more ownership.
notes.example: The team that writes a feature also deploys it and answers for how it performs in production.

notes.front: What is DevSecOps?
notes.back: DevOps extended to include security: a cultural merger of development, operations and security responsibilities.
notes.explanation: Security is built into automated workflows, enforcing policy without blocking developers.
notes.example: Automated security checks that run every time code changes, with clear advice on how to fix what they find.

notes.front: What does “shift left” mean?
notes.back: Doing testing, security and other practices early in the software development lifecycle, rather than towards the end.
notes.explanation: Picture the lifecycle as a line running left to right: defects found late, or after deployment, are harder and costlier to fix.
notes.example: Reviewing security during design instead of just before release.

notes.front: What is site reliability engineering (SRE)?
notes.back: A discipline combining operations and software engineering: instead of product features, engineers build systems that keep applications running.
notes.explanation: The system continuously measures itself and points engineers to when, where and how to fix problems.
notes.example: An engineer automates recovery from a common fault instead of fixing it by hand each time.

notes.front: What is platform engineering?
notes.back: Building tools and processes that let software developers serve themselves throughout the software creation journey.
notes.explanation: It hides infrastructure complexity and automates repetitive tasks, such as setting up environments, so developers can focus on code.
notes.example: A self-service portal where a developer gets a ready-made test environment in minutes.

notes.front: What is chaos engineering?
notes.back: Experimenting on a distributed system in production to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent, unexpected conditions.
notes.explanation: Engineers inject failures on purpose to check that the system heals itself and customers do not notice.
notes.example: Switching off a random server during the working day to see whether the service stays up.

notes.front: What is WebAssembly (Wasm)?
notes.back: A compact code format into which programs written in C, C++ or Rust can be turned, so they run fast and the same way anywhere.
notes.explanation: It runs at near-native speed and behaves the same across browsers, operating systems and devices, including outside the web.
notes.example: A photo editor written in C++ running inside a web browser.

notes.front: What is the kernel of an operating system?
notes.back: The operating system’s core: the only part with unlimited access to the hardware.
notes.explanation: Ordinary applications run outside it, in “user space”, and must ask the kernel whenever they need higher permissions or the hardware.
notes.example: A program that sends data over the network asks the Linux kernel, the core of Linux, to do it.

notes.front: What is eBPF?
notes.back: A way to run small, walled-off programs inside the Linux kernel without changing the kernel or adding riskier add-on code (kernel modules).
notes.explanation: A checker (the verifier) vets each program before it runs, which makes it safer than kernel modules for networking, security and observability tools.
notes.example: A small program added to the kernel to watch network traffic, with no change to the kernel itself.

notes.front: What is gRPC?
notes.back: A way for programs to talk to each other over a network using a compact message format that computers read faster than text.
notes.explanation: You define once how programs should talk, and code for each supported programming language is generated from that definition.
notes.example: A driver’s phone sends location updates while receiving new passenger requests at the same time.

notes.front: What must be true of an application before it can scale horizontally?
notes.back: It must be able to run as several copies, which may mean changing its code.
notes.explanation: Vertical scaling avoids this: the same application simply gets a bigger machine.

notes.front: What are the drawbacks of vertical scaling for a single machine?
notes.back: It is time-consuming, needs downtime, and quickly reaches its limit.
notes.explanation: Distributed systems avoid these limits by scaling horizontally, adding nodes when needed.

notes.front: What can autoscaling be configured to react to?
notes.back: Metrics such as memory use or processing time.
notes.explanation: Managed cloud services typically offer autoscaling, with more options than most on-premises set-ups.

notes.front: What is the goal of cloud native applications with respect to reliability?
notes.back: To be inherently reliable: to keep working as infrastructure changes and components fail.
notes.explanation: A system that fails easily and needs operators to keep it running is unreliable.

notes.front: Which two kinds of signal are used to observe a system?
notes.back: Low-level signals such as CPU time and memory, and higher-level ones such as API response times and errors.
notes.explanation: Tools that collect these signals are called observability tools.

notes.front: What does a declarative description separate?
notes.back: The configuration (the desired state) from the implementation used to reach it, such as commands, API calls or scripts.
notes.explanation: That is why you can change how a system is built without changing what you asked for.

notes.front: What record do imperative commands leave of earlier configurations?
notes.back: None: they provide no history of previous configurations beyond what is live.
notes.explanation: They also do not fit change-review processes or provide an audit trail.

notes.front: What does a self-healing system do when its actual state differs from the desired state?
notes.back: It takes corrective action, such as starting new instances when too few are running.
notes.explanation: The system actively checks its actual state against the desired state, and acts on any difference.

notes.front: Why might a team deliberately start with a monolith?
notes.back: It is the simplest way to get an app running; microservices built before the product proves valuable may waste effort.
notes.explanation: A successful monolith can later be broken into microservices.

notes.front: What cost does a microservices architecture bring?
notes.back: Operational overhead: the number of things to deploy and keep track of grows by an order of magnitude.
notes.explanation: Many cloud native technologies exist to make microservices easier to deploy and manage.

notes.front: What two risks does a tightly coupled architecture carry?
notes.back: Cascading failures, and the need for coordinated rollouts that slow developers down.
notes.explanation: In return, it is usually faster and simpler to build at first.

notes.front: How do you make a lasting change to immutable infrastructure?
notes.back: By creating a new version and replacing the old one, not by editing what is running.
notes.explanation: Unauthorised changes are either blocked or automatically overwritten.

notes.front: What does immutable infrastructure combined with version control give you?
notes.back: A durable audit log of every authorised change to the system.
notes.explanation: The automation that creates the infrastructure is stored as code in version control, for example in Git.

notes.front: What does infrastructure as code replace?
notes.back: Setting up infrastructure manually, usually through shell scripts or other configuration tools.
notes.explanation: Manual changes are not reproducible, hit scale limits quickly and introduce misconfiguration.

notes.front: Are multitenancy and SaaS the same thing?
notes.back: No. SaaS is very often multitenant, but the two terms are not synonyms.
notes.explanation: Multitenancy is about one installation serving many tenants; SaaS is about software delivered and run by a provider.

notes.front: How is serverless computing charged?
notes.back: Pay per use: you pay when your code runs, not for servers kept waiting.
notes.explanation: In IaaS, by contrast, you commit to capacity and pay for it whether or not it is used.

notes.front: Which range of cloud services can the term “serverless” cover?
notes.back: Services from PaaS to SaaS that share its traits: no servers to manage, automatic scaling and pay-per-use.
notes.explanation: Serverless is an umbrella term; FaaS is one specific model within it.

notes.front: In the CNCF definition, what kind of systems characterise cloud native?
notes.back: Loosely coupled systems that work together securely, resiliently, manageably, sustainably and observably.
notes.explanation: The definition names public, private and hybrid clouds as the environments.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition says cloud native systems interoperate in a way that is sustainable, observable and three other things. Which three?
notes.back: Secure, resilient and manageable.
notes.explanation: All five qualities describe how the loosely coupled parts work together.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition says cloud native systems interoperate in a way that is secure, resilient, manageable and two other things. Which two?
notes.back: Sustainable and observable.
notes.explanation: All five qualities describe how the loosely coupled parts work together.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: According to the CNCF definition, what does cloud native allow, when combined with robust automation?
notes.back: Frequent, predictable, high-impact changes with minimal toil and clear separation of concerns.
notes.explanation: This is the definition’s stated benefit of cloud native practices. Toil means repetitive manual work; separation of concerns means each part does one job.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Benefits of Cloud Native”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: Which version of the CNCF Cloud Native Definition is current, and when was it approved?
notes.back: Version 1.1, approved on 26 February 2024.
notes.explanation: It was approved by the CNCF Technical Oversight Committee and Governing Board.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: Does the CNCF definition’s list of typical cloud native technologies claim to be complete?
notes.back: No: it says the list is non-exhaustive.
notes.explanation: Cloud native systems use “some combination” of the listed technologies.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition lists, among typical cloud native technologies, the approach of splitting an app into small independent services. What is it called?
notes.back: Microservices.
notes.explanation: It is one of the technologies the definition names; the list is non-exhaustive.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition lists, among typical cloud native technologies, one installation serving many separate users. What is it called?
notes.back: Multi-tenancy (multitenancy).
notes.explanation: It is one of the technologies the definition names; the list is non-exhaustive.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition lists, among typical cloud native technologies, infrastructure that is replaced rather than changed. What is it called?
notes.back: Immutable infrastructure.
notes.explanation: It is one of the technologies the definition names; the list is non-exhaustive.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: The CNCF definition lists, among typical cloud native technologies, computing where the provider hides and manages the servers. What is it called?
notes.back: Serverless.
notes.explanation: It is one of the technologies the definition names; the list is non-exhaustive.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: Which style of API does the CNCF definition list among typical cloud native technologies?
notes.back: Declarative APIs.
notes.explanation: A declarative API accepts a description of the desired state, rather than step-by-step commands.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: What problem of traditional organisations did DevOps set out to fix?
notes.back: Work split between many groups, causing numerous handoffs, long lead times and a lack of ownership.
notes.explanation: Each team only passed its piece on to the next queue, so problems were hard to trace.

notes.front: How does the glossary distinguish SRE from DevOps?
notes.back: DevOps focuses on getting code to production; SRE makes sure code running in production works properly.
notes.explanation: Both aim at reliable software, from different ends of the path.
notes.contrast: Getting code into production, versus keeping it working there.

notes.front: Are serverless and FaaS the same concept?
notes.back: No. They are often used interchangeably, but FaaS is the specific model of event-triggered, short-lived functions.
notes.explanation: Serverless is the broader idea of hiding servers from the user.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Function as a Service (FaaS)”

notes.front: Traffic doubles, so an operator adds four more identical servers behind the same app. Which kind of scaling is this?
notes.back: Horizontal scaling.
notes.explanation: Adding nodes spreads the load; making one server bigger would be vertical scaling.

notes.front: A database server is moved to a machine with twice the CPU and memory. Which kind of scaling is this?
notes.back: Vertical scaling.
notes.explanation: Capacity grows by making the individual node more powerful.

notes.front: Every evening, servers are added as viewers arrive and removed once they leave, with no one intervening. What is this?
notes.back: Autoscaling.
notes.explanation: Resources follow demand automatically instead of being sized for the peak.

notes.front: A system can handle more users simply by adding capacity, with no redesign. Which property does it have?
notes.back: Scalability.
notes.explanation: A scalable system makes it easy to add capacity.

notes.front: Engineers must restart a system by hand whenever one of its components fails. Which property is it lacking?
notes.back: Reliability.
notes.explanation: A reliable system keeps working as components fail, without manual intervention.

notes.front: A company can move its application to another cloud provider with only small changes. Which property does the application have?
notes.back: Portability.
notes.explanation: Portable software avoids lock-in to one provider, operating system or vendor.

notes.front: Users report slow pages, but the team has no data showing which part is slow. Which property does the system lack?
notes.back: Observability.
notes.explanation: An observable system yields meaningful, actionable data about its state to the people who run it.

notes.front: An engineer writes a file saying “three web servers, version 2” and a tool makes it so. Declarative or imperative?
notes.back: Declarative.
notes.explanation: The file states the desired result and leaves the steps to the tool.

notes.front: An engineer types “add a server”, then “restart server 2”, then “delete server 1”. Declarative or imperative?
notes.back: Imperative.
notes.explanation: Each command states an operation to perform, not the end state wanted.

notes.front: A configuration says five copies of an app should run; four are running. Which is the desired state, and which the current state?
notes.back: Five copies is the desired state; four is the current state.
notes.explanation: Automation acts to bring the current state closer to the desired state.

notes.front: One copy of an application crashes at 3 a.m.; by morning a replacement is running and nobody was paged. Which property made this happen?
notes.back: Self-healing.
notes.explanation: The system compared actual with desired state and took corrective action on its own.

notes.front: A two-person start-up is testing whether anyone wants its product. Which architecture does the glossary suggest starting with?
notes.back: A monolithic application.
notes.explanation: Building microservices before the product has proved valuable may waste engineering effort.

notes.front: After a marketing campaign, sign-ups spike while streaming stays flat. Which architecture lets you scale only the sign-up part?
notes.back: A microservices architecture.
notes.explanation: In a monolith, the whole application would have to be scaled, which wastes resources.

notes.front: Changing the format of one component’s data forces three other components to change and release together. What kind of architecture is this?
notes.back: Tightly coupled.
notes.explanation: Its components are interdependent, so a change ripples through them.

notes.front: Each team builds, deploys and scales its own component, which others use without depending on its internals. What kind of architecture is this?
notes.back: Loosely coupled.
notes.explanation: Components are built independently of one another.

notes.front: A server needs a security fix. Under immutable infrastructure, what should the team do?
notes.back: Build a new, fixed version and replace the old server with it.
notes.explanation: Changing the running server in place would break the principle that deployed infrastructure is not changed.

notes.front: A team keeps files describing all its servers, subnets and load balancers in Git, and builds environments from them. What practice is this?
notes.back: Infrastructure as code.
notes.explanation: The files give a single source of truth for the configuration.

notes.front: A rule forbidding secrets in source code is written in a machine-readable file and checked automatically. What practice is this?
notes.back: Policy as code.
notes.explanation: It replaces policies documented only in human-readable form.

notes.front: An accounting application serves 500 companies from one installation; no company can see another’s data. What is this?
notes.back: Multitenancy.
notes.explanation: Each tenant gets a separate environment within the shared installation.

notes.front: Code runs only when a photo is uploaded, resizes it, then stops; the team pays nothing while no photos arrive. What model is this?
notes.back: FaaS (Function as a Service).
notes.explanation: Event-triggered, short-lived functions with automatic scaling are the core of FaaS.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Function as a Service (FaaS)”

notes.front: A team deploys its app to a provider that manages all the servers, scales them automatically and bills only for use. What is this approach called?
notes.back: Serverless.
notes.explanation: Serverless hides the servers; operational management falls to the provider.

notes.front: A factory analyses its sensor data on site and sends only results to head office. What approach is this?
notes.back: Edge computing.
notes.explanation: Computing near the data source reduces delay compared with a central data centre.

notes.front: An online order is published to a central hub, which routes it to the stock, payment and email services. What kind of architecture is this?
notes.back: Event-driven architecture.
notes.explanation: Producers publish events and a central hub routes them to consumers, keeping services decoupled.

notes.front: One team writes, tests, deploys and runs its service in production, instead of handing it to a separate operations group. What methodology is this?
notes.back: DevOps.
notes.explanation: One team owns the whole lifecycle, which minimises handoffs.

notes.front: A team moves its security testing from the week before release to the design and coding stages. What is this practice called?
notes.back: Shift left.
notes.explanation: Earlier stages sit to the “left” of a lifecycle drawn from left to right.

notes.front: Development, operations and security staff share responsibility, with security checks built into the automated release process. What is this called?
notes.back: DevSecOps.
notes.explanation: It extends DevOps to include security priorities with minimal disruption to developers.

notes.front: A team builds a self-service portal from which developers create their own test environments. What discipline is this?
notes.back: Platform engineering.
notes.explanation: It gives developers pre-built tools and automated processes so they can focus on code.

notes.front: Engineers deliberately shut down random servers in production to check that customers do not notice. What discipline is this?
notes.back: Chaos engineering.
notes.explanation: Chaos experiments inject failures to verify the system can heal itself.

notes.front: An application was designed to use its cloud’s resources and scaling, and restarts itself automatically after failures. How would you describe it?
notes.back: As a cloud native application.
notes.explanation: Apps that need manual intervention to start cannot scale or restart automatically.

notes.front: Microservices, immutable infrastructure and serverless are all examples of what, taken together?
notes.back: Cloud native technologies, also called the cloud native stack.
notes.explanation: Each solves a specific problem; together they help build loosely coupled, resilient, manageable and observable systems.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Cloud Native Tech”; CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1, “Definition” (which lists serverless)

notes.front: A company deploys workloads across public and private clouds, at scale, using automated and repeatable processes. Which term from the CNCF describes these practices?
notes.back: Cloud native.
notes.explanation: The CNCF definition centres on programmatic, repeatable development and deployment in any kind of cloud.
notes.source: CNCF Cloud Native Definition v1.1 (CNCF Technical Oversight Committee), “Definition”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
notes.back: Horizontal adds more nodes; vertical adds CPU and memory to existing nodes.
notes.explanation: Horizontal may need code that runs as several copies; vertical needs no code change but soon hits a limit.

notes.front: What is the difference between declarative and imperative management?
notes.back: Declarative describes the desired end state; imperative gives commands for each operation to perform.
notes.explanation: With declarative configuration, the system works out the steps itself.
notes.contrast: What you want, versus what to do.

notes.front: What is the difference between a monolithic application and a microservices architecture?
notes.back: A monolith is one deployable program; microservices split the app into independent services, each deployed and scaled separately.
notes.explanation: Monoliths are simpler to start; microservices are easier to update and scale piece by piece, at a cost in operational overhead.
notes.contrast: One program, versus many independent services.

notes.front: What is the difference between loosely and tightly coupled architectures?
notes.back: Loosely coupled components are built independently; tightly coupled ones depend on each other, so changes ripple.
notes.explanation: Tight coupling is quicker to build; loose coupling lets teams deploy and scale independently.

notes.front: What does DevSecOps add to DevOps?
notes.back: Security responsibilities, merged into the shared development and operations culture and its automated workflows.
notes.explanation: A fast release process that ignores security can weaken an organisation’s security posture.
notes.contrast: Development and operations, versus development, security and operations.

notes.front: What is the difference between an event-driven architecture and event streaming?
notes.back: Event-driven architecture routes events from producers to consumers through a hub; event streaming continuously broadcasts events to subscribers.
notes.explanation: Both treat changes as events; streaming is about the continuous flow of them.
notes.contrast: Routing events, versus broadcasting a continuous stream.
